title: There’s Never a New Middle East
gist: Steven Simon argues the U.S.-Iran war and Hormuz fight will not produce a 'new Middle East': regional states will look much as before, Gulf economies are contracting sharply, and the real change is that the Middle East is absorbing U.S. naval power and reshaping U.S. posture in Asia. He expects the next administration to test less intervention.

insights.claim: U.S. leaders have repeatedly predicted a transformed Middle East after Iraq 2003, Lebanon 2006, the Arab Spring and Hamas's 2023 attack, and the current Iran war is generating the same prediction that will again fail to pan out.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Discount narratives of regional transformation priced into Gulf/Israel risk assets; base case is continuity.
insights.quote: Washington’s fantasies of transformation keep failing to pan out.
insights.locator: This year’s op-eds and magazine features

insights.claim: Decisive change requires both a real preponderance of U.S. military power and the ability to convert it into enduring political arrangements; the author says the U.S. has imagined possessing both while having neither.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Military wins should not be extrapolated into durable political settlements.
insights.quote: The United States has imagined itself as wielding both attributes while possessing neither.
insights.locator: Bloody and chaotic events like the Iran war

insights.claim: The weakness and fragmentation of regional states makes it harder, not easier, for an outside power to impose its will.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: State fragility raises, not lowers, the cost of intervention outcomes.
insights.quote: the weakness and fragmentation of regional states makes it more, not less, difficult for an outside power to impose its will
insights.locator: On the other side, adversaries have agency

insights.claim: After the war, Iran will still be a poor, militarized oil exporter allied with China and Russia and close to Iraq, i.e. little changed from before the war.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Do not expect regime change or a structurally new Iranian oil supply picture.
insights.quote: Iran will still be a poor, militarized oil exporter with two good friends—China and Russia
insights.locator: When the war ends, as it eventually will

insights.claim: Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and Jordan are expected to emerge essentially unchanged; Lebanon remains stuck trying to satisfy the IMF without a parliament willing to allocate banking-system losses, and Egypt remains propped up by Gulf largesse.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Lebanon restructuring and Egypt's Gulf dependence remain unresolved credit stories.
insights.locator: Lebanon will still be living with

insights.claim: Somaliland is a rare beneficiary, collecting strategic rent from the UAE, Israel and the U.S. as a counterweight to Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Red Sea chokepoint geography is monetizable for small actors; watch Somaliland basing deals.
insights.quote: But one breakaway enclave doth not a new Middle East make.
insights.locator: True, there is the odd beneficiary

insights.claim: The IMF projects 2026 GDP contractions of 16.7% for Kuwait, 15.6% for Qatar, 11.3% for Bahrain and smaller declines for the UAE and Saudi Arabia; every Gulf state except Oman will shrink this year.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Severe Gulf output shock; sovereign/financial exposures to Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain at risk.
insights.quote: The IMF projects contractions of 16.7 percent for Kuwait, 15.6 percent for Qatar, 11.3 percent for Bahrain
insights.locator: What about the Arab side of the Gulf?

insights.claim: The IMF's expected sharp Gulf rebound in 2027 depends on the generous assumption that Hormuz traffic normalizes during 2027.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Gulf rebound forecasts carry downside risk if strait disruption persists.
insights.quote: only on the generous assumption that traffic through the strait returns to normal during 2027
insights.locator: What about the Arab side of the Gulf?

insights.claim: Crude flows out of the Gulf are already back at prewar levels, moving under U.S. escort, though the process is cumbersome.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Physical oil supply has largely normalized; residual risk premium tied to escalation, not current volumes.
insights.quote: Crude flows are already at prewar levels even if the process of moving it is cumbersome.
insights.locator: What about the Arab side of the Gulf?

insights.claim: Gulf states are touting bypass pipelines (Abqaiq–Yanbu, Habshan–Fujairah, Basra–Baniyas) for export redundancy, but the author expects most will never be built.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of pipeline megaproject announcements as investable themes.
insights.quote: Plans for such projects are nothing new for them, and most will probably never be built.
insights.locator: Most of these states are talking

insights.claim: Gulf states will rush to rebuild air defenses, viewing the U.S. as ineffectual at war but still an eager arms dealer, intelligence source and defense-industrial partner.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Supports Gulf air-defense procurement demand for U.S. defense contractors.
insights.quote: relatively ineffectual as a wager of wars but still an eager arms dealer
insights.locator: Most of these states are talking

insights.claim: One path is a concessionary cease-fire restoring Hormuz traffic; a Democratic Congress could hasten it via funding fights, though Trump would veto a war powers resolution and Democrats likely lack override votes.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Watch congressional war-funding fights as a catalyst for de-escalation.
insights.locator: How does this war end?

insights.claim: A funding fight gives Trump a win-win: he could blame Democrats for losing the war rather than owning the loss himself.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Political incentives favor an exit framed as Congress's fault.
insights.locator: A fight over funding would still

insights.claim: In a settlement, Gulf states would revert to hedging—side deals with Iran to open the strait while keeping U.S. intelligence, technology and weapons—possibly even without the Fifth Fleet in Bahrain, resembling an over-the-horizon/offshore-balancing posture.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Gulf-Iran rapprochement and reduced U.S. footprint are plausible post-war outcomes.
insights.locator: A fight over funding would still

insights.claim: Bessent and Hegseth appear to prefer an open-ended economic-attrition war; Bessent's satellite imagery shows no tankers at Kharg Island while escorted Gulf crude moves at or above prewar volumes.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Iranian export blockade is effective; Iran's oil revenues are being choked.
insights.quote: Bessent’s satellite imagery shows no tankers at Kharg Island
insights.locator: The other way is that the war does not end

insights.claim: Iran will respond to attrition by raising costs for Washington—Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, attacks at Dhahran and Dammam, threats to U.S. bases—keeping open the risk of escalation Trump wants to avoid; a third carrier group is en route.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Tail risk of escalation and attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure remains live.
insights.locator: Why settle? Because Iran gets a vote.

themes.theme: Middle East remaking U.S. Asia posture

insights.claim: With the Theodore Roosevelt in the Arabian Sea, three quarters of the Navy's deployed carriers will be committed to the war, leaving no U.S. carrier in the Western Pacific.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Reduced U.S. deterrence in Asia raises Taiwan/South China Sea risk premia.
insights.quote: there is now no U.S. carrier in the Western Pacific
insights.locator: If the war does drag on

insights.claim: The Middle East is remaking U.S. strategy rather than the reverse, by absorbing so much U.S. power that it changes America's position in Asia.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Second-order: Mideast war weakens U.S. posture vs. China.
insights.quote: The Middle East is remaking U.S. strategy, rather than the other way around.
insights.locator: If the war does drag on

insights.claim: The war has accelerated the souring of American opinion on Israel, narrowing support for the relationship and turning it into a partisan football, amid the impression Netanyahu lured Trump into the war.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: U.S. support for Israel is becoming partisan and less durable.
insights.locator: The result has been catastrophic for Gazans

insights.claim: The next U.S. administration will likely test less intervention, facing a public that sees the Iran war as a mistake, colossal debt squeezing defense budgets, and a Congress prioritizing the Western Pacific and Europe.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Expect pressure on Middle East defense spending and a pivot of resources to Asia/Europe.
insights.quote: Colossal debt and demand for spending on the lives of ordinary people will squeeze the defense budget.
insights.locator: That experiment is likely to be run

insights.claim: War-induced inflation is hurting U.S. families, part of the war's domestic cost.
insights.speaker: Steven Simon
insights.so_what: Energy-driven inflation remains a political constraint on the war.
insights.quote: families back home struggling with war-induced inflation
insights.locator: But restraint has never really been
